analysis.one_liner: Lets the FDA deny and punish citizen petitions filed mainly to delay generic drug approval.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would curb petitions used to hold generic drugs off the market, was referred to the Senate HELP Committee on March 3, 2021 and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Brand-name drug companies sometimes file petitions with the FDA—called citizen petitions—claiming safety or manufacturing concerns about a proposed generic or biosimilar, primarily to delay its approval and keep their monopoly going. This bill would let the FDA reject such petitions as delay tactics even if they also raise valid issues, refer them to the FTC, require anyone challenging a generic approval in court to first file a petition with all their arguments, and impose 60-day filing deadlines. It would cut through a tactic used to keep cheaper versions of drugs off the market.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who need cheaper generic drugs and biosimilars. Generic and biosimilar makers would also benefit from faster approvals and fewer delay-driven petitions and lawsuits, and the FTC would gain new referrals of anticompetitive petition behavior.

how_it_helps.text: Currently the FDA may deny a petition as a delay attempt only if it fails on both counts—being submitted primarily to delay AND lacking valid scientific or regulatory issues; the bill allows denial on either basis alone.
The FDA must establish procedures to refer any petition determined to be primarily for delay to the Federal Trade Commission, which can police anticompetitive conduct.

Before suing the FDA to block a generic or biosimilar's approval, a third party must first file a citizen petition containing all the information and arguments behind the lawsuit, and petitions must be filed within 60 days of when the filer knew the relevant information.
Courts must dismiss lawsuits that bypass the petition process, or that are filed too late, preventing late-stage litigation ambushes against approved generics.

The bill lists detailed factors the FDA may weigh in judging whether a petition's primary purpose is delay—including serial petitions, timing near approval dates, lack of supporting data, and requests for more onerous testing standards than the original drug faced.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies would lose a tool that can extend their market exclusivity beyond patents, likely facing sooner generic and biosimilar competition and lower prices. Petitioners with genuine safety concerns would face tighter deadlines and more scrutiny, but the bill preserves the right to file and litigate legitimate petitions.

drawbacks.text: Some citizen petitions raise legitimate safety and quality concerns, and a faster, stricter process raises the risk that a real problem with a generic gets screened out or time-barred before it is fully aired.
The 60-day filing deadline could be difficult for petitioners who learn of problems through complex supply chains, and courts must dismiss with prejudice—permanently—any suit filed late.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits—faster access to lower-cost generics in a market where some brand drugs face no generic competition for years past patent expiry—clearly outweigh the costs. The bill preserves the petition and lawsuit process for legitimate concerns while removing its use as a pure delay tool. Legitimate safety objections are still heard; they just have to be raised promptly and completely.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Introduced March 3, 2021 by Sen. Jeanne Shaheen with bipartisan cosponsors Sens. Cassidy, Bennet, and Rubio.
Read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day—the only action besides introduction.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action occurred; the Congress ended January 3, 2023 without further movement.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies are better off, since the tool the bill would have curtailed—the delay petition—remains available unchanged. Patients continue paying brand-name prices where generic competition was delayed.

for.name: Sen. Jeanne Shaheen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to curb petitions used to delay generic approval.

for.name: Sens. Bill Cassidy (R-LA), Michael Bennet (D-CO), and Marco Rubio (R-FL)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it bipartisan support from the start.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never took it up—no hearing, markup, or vote in the 117th Congress.

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Industry with a stake in delaying generic competition
against.what_they_did: The bill targets a practice associated with brand-name firms, which oppose curbs on the citizen-petition tool; its activity at the committee helps explain the bill going nowhere.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship—one Democrat sponsor plus one more Democrat and two Republicans cosponsoring—but that support never translated into committee action.

industries.note: Faster FDA approval of their applications and court rules that block late challenges would let them bring lower-cost drugs to market sooner, directly lowering prices for patients.
They would lose a key tool—citizen petitions and follow-on lawsuits used to delay generic and biosimilar approvals—shortening periods of monopoly pricing on their drugs.
